title: The Sūtra of Individual Liberation
explainer: The Prātimokṣa Sūtra, known in Tibetan as the Sosor Tharpa'i Do (སོ་སོར་ཐར་པའི་མདོ་), or in English as the Sūtra of Individual Liberation, is one of the most foundational texts of Buddhist monastic life, setting out the rules of conduct and training that govern the lives of fully ordained monks. It belongs to the Vinaya, the broad category of canonical literature concerned with monastic discipline, and takes the form of a sūtra whose verses and injunctions are traditionally recited at communal confession ceremonies held twice monthly within the monastic community. Opening with a homage to the Buddha as the Omniscient One who discovered the treasury of the Three Jewels and crossed the ocean of suffering, the text frames its detailed disciplinary code within a devotional and doctrinal vision of the Buddha's incomparable wisdom and compassion. This text is Toh 2 in the Kangyur, where it is classified among the Vinaya scriptures.

title: The Sūtra of Individual Liberation for Fully Ordained Nuns
explainer: Toh 4 in the Kangyur is the Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra, known in Tibetan as the Dge slong ma'i so sor thar pa'i mdo, or in English as the Sūtra of Individual Liberation for Fully Ordained Nuns. It is a Vinaya text — a code of monastic discipline — setting out the rules of individual liberation, the prātimokṣa, specifically for fully ordained Buddhist nuns, the bhikṣuṇīs. The text opens with verses of homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha before proceeding to enumerate the precepts that govern the conduct and spiritual life of nuns within the monastic community. As one of the foundational disciplinary scriptures, it belongs to the Vinaya section of the Kangyur, the collection of texts attributed to the Buddha himself.

The Noble Perfection of Wisdom: A Verse Condensation
explainer: Toh 13 in the Kangyur is the Āryaprajñāpāramitāsaṃcayagāthā, known in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa sdud pa tshigs su bcad pa, and rendered in English as The Noble Perfection of Wisdom: A Verse Condensation. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of sūtras, one of the most important groupings in the Kangyur, and presents the profound teachings on prajñāpāramitā — the wisdom gone beyond — in metrical verse form rather than the extended prose dialogues characteristic of longer works in this cycle. As its title indicates, the text functions as a poetic summary or condensation of the Perfection of Wisdom teachings, covering themes such as omniscience, the nature of emptiness, and the path of the bodhisattva. It is among the earliest and most studied verse formulations of prajñāpāramitā doctrine and has been widely used across Buddhist traditions as a concise yet comprehensive expression of these teachings.

title: The perfection of wisdom teachings the questions of suvikrantavikramin
The Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Five Hundred Lines
explainer: Toh 15 in the Kangyur is the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Five Hundred Lines, known in Sanskrit as the Āryapañcaśatikāprajñāpāramitā and in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa lnga brgya pa. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of sūtras, a body of canonical Buddhist scripture that explores the nature of emptiness and the transcendent wisdom cultivated on the bodhisattva path. Like others in this genre, it takes the form of a discourse delivered by the Buddha — here on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagṛha — in which he instructs the Venerable Subhūti on the insubstantial nature of the aggregates, sense bases, and all conditioned phenomena. As one of the shorter Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, it distills these profound themes concisely, sitting within the broader collection of Perfection of Wisdom texts that forms a central section of the Kangyur.

title: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom Called the Diamond Cutter
explainer: The Diamond Cutter Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-mahāyāna-sūtra and in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa rdo rje gcod pa, is one of the most celebrated texts in the Mahāyāna Buddhist tradition. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of sūtras and teaches the nature of emptiness and non-attachment, famously using the image of a diamond or thunderbolt that cuts through illusion to convey how wisdom severs all conceptual clinging, including attachment to the very teachings themselves. The text is structured as a dialogue between the Buddha and his disciple Subhūti, set in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada near Śrāvastī, and unfolds through a series of penetrating questions and answers about the nature of bodhisattvas, merit, and ultimate reality. It is Toh 16 in the Kangyur, preserved among the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras, and has been among the most widely studied and revered scriptures across the Mahāyāna world for well over a millennium.

title: The Noble One Hundred and Fifty Modes of the Perfection of Wisdom
explainer: Toh 17 in the Kangyur is a Perfection of Wisdom sūtra known in English as "The Noble One Hundred and Fifty Modes of the Perfection of Wisdom," in Sanskrit as the Āryaprajñāpāramitānayaśatapañcāśatikā, and in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i tshul brgya lnga bcu pa. It belongs to the Prajñāpāramitā class of canonical Buddhist texts, which expound the doctrine of the perfection of wisdom and the nature of emptiness as the foundation of the bodhisattva path. The text opens in the traditional sūtra style with the Buddha as its central figure, described in richly elaborated terms as the sovereign of great yogins, the mother of all Tathāgatas, and the embodiment of omniscient primordial wisdom. As one of the shorter Perfection of Wisdom sūtras preserved in the Kangyur, it presents the teaching of transcendent wisdom through a structured enumeration of its modes or aspects, situating it within the broader tradition of texts that systematically analyze the nature and practice of prajñāpāramitā.

title: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom of the Blessed Lady in Fifty Lines
explainer: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom of the Blessed Lady in Fifty Lines, known in Sanskrit as the Āryabhagavatī-prajñāpāramitā-pañcāśatikā and in Tibetan as Phags pa bcom ldan 'das ma shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa lnga bcu pa, is a short Prajñāpāramitā sūtra belonging to the Perfection of Wisdom class of Mahāyāna scriptures. As its title indicates, the text is a condensed teaching on the perfection of wisdom, delivered by the Buddha at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha to an assembly of monks, bodhisattvas, and various divine and worldly beings, with the venerable Subhūti as the primary interlocutor. The discourse addresses those wishing to train at the levels of śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva, offering a succinct distillation of prajñāpāramitā doctrine. It is catalogued as Toh 18 in the Kangyur, where it forms part of the collection of Perfection of Wisdom sūtras.

title: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom Called Kauśika
explainer: Toh 19 in the Kangyur is a sūtra known in English as the Noble Perfection of Wisdom Called Kauśika, in Sanskrit as the Ārya Kauśika Prajñāpāramitā, and in Tibetan as Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa kau shi ka. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of texts and presents the Buddha teaching Śakra, lord of the gods — whose epithet Kauśika gives the text its name — on the nature of the Perfection of Wisdom as beyond duality, signs, and all conceptual elaboration. The setting is Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, where the Buddha addresses a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, and the text unfolds as a direct discourse on the ineffable character of wisdom that transcends taking up or casting aside. As a relatively concise Prajñāpāramitā sūtra, it sits within the broader collection of Perfection of Wisdom scriptures in the Kangyur.

title: The Twenty-Five Gateways of the Perfection of Wisdom
explainer: Toh 20 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-pañcaviṃśatika-prajñāpāramitā-mukha, in Tibetan as the Shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i sgo nyi shu rtsa lnga pa, and in English as The Twenty-Five Gateways of the Perfection of Wisdom. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom genre, a major class of Mahāyāna scripture concerned with the nature of prajñāpāramitā, or transcendent wisdom, and the path of the bodhisattva. The text opens with the Buddha dwelling on the summit of Mount Meru, surrounded by a vast assembly of bodhisattvas, gods, and other beings within a great maṇḍala, and proceeds to expound the perfection of wisdom through twenty-five thematic gateways or modes of entry. As its catalog number indicates, it is Toh 20 in the Kangyur, placed among the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras that form one of the most extensive and central sections of that collection.

title: Heart of the Blessed Lady, the Perfection of Wisdom
explainer: Toh 21 in the Kangyur is the Heart Sūtra, known in Sanskrit as the Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā Hṛdaya and in Tibetan as the Bcom ldan 'das ma shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i snying po, meaning "The Heart of the Blessed Lady, the Perfection of Wisdom." It is one of the most celebrated and widely recited texts in all of Buddhist literature, belonging to the Prajñāpāramitā, or Perfection of Wisdom, class of sūtras, and it distills the vast teachings on emptiness and wisdom into a remarkably compact form. The text presents the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara's insight into the emptiness of the five aggregates, culminating in the famous mantra that encapsulates the path to liberation. As a sūtra attributed to the speech of the Buddha, it belongs to the Kangyur, the Tibetan canonical collection of translated words of the Buddha, and sits within the broader Prajñāpāramitā section of that canon.

title: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Few Syllables
explainer: Toh 22 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in Sanskrit as the Āryasvalpaakṣaraprajñāpāramitā and in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa yi ge nyung ngu, meaning in English the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Few Syllables. As its name suggests, it is a brief prajñāpāramitā scripture — one of the shorter texts belonging to the Perfection of Wisdom class — that distills the essence of the vast prajñāpāramitā literature into a compact teaching on the nature of emptiness and awakening. The sūtra opens with the Buddha residing on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, where the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rises to deliver its core instruction. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom section of the Kangyur, standing within a rich tradition of sūtras that range from enormously expansive to highly condensed formulations of the same profound insight.

title: The Perfection of Wisdom in a Single Syllable, the Mother of All Tathāgatas
explainer: Toh 23 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as "The Perfection of Wisdom in a Single Syllable, the Mother of All Tathāgatas," in Sanskrit as the Eka Akṣarī Mātā Nāma Sarva Tathāgata Prajñāpāramitā, and in Tibetan as the Deshyin shekpa thamché kyi yum yigé chungngü shyejawa. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom, or Prajñāpāramitā, class of texts — a body of Mahāyāna literature concerned with the nature of wisdom and emptiness as the path to awakening. This remarkably concise sūtra takes the form of a teaching given by the Buddha on Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha, addressed to his attendant Ānanda, in which the entirety of the Perfection of Wisdom is distilled into a single syllable for the benefit of all sentient beings. As Toh 23 in the Kangyur, it is counted among the canonical scriptures preserved in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition, sitting within the broader Prajñāpāramitā section of that collection.

title: The Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called the Perfection of Wisdom in Seven Hundred Lines
explainer: Toh 24 in the Kangyur is the Noble Great Vehicle Sūtra Called the Perfection of Wisdom in Seven Hundred Lines, known in Sanskrit as the Ārya-saptaśatikā-prajñāpāramitā-mahāyāna-sūtra and in Tibetan as the Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa bdun brgya pa. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of Mahāyāna sūtras and, like others in this genre, expounds the doctrine of prajñāpāramitā — the perfection of wisdom that perceives the empty nature of all phenomena. The text opens in the familiar sūtra style, with the Buddha residing at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove accompanied by a great assembly of monks and a vast gathering of bodhisattvas including Mañjuśrī and Maitreya, pointing to the dialogical treatment of wisdom that characterizes the Perfection of Wisdom literature. As one of the shorter prajñāpāramitā scriptures, it distills key insights of the tradition in a relatively compact form, situating it within the rich spectrum of Perfection of Wisdom texts preserved in the Kangyur.

title: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom: A Text of One Hundred and Eight Names
explainer: Toh 25 in the Kangyur is a short liturgical scripture known in English as "The Noble Perfection of Wisdom: A Text of One Hundred and Eight Names," corresponding to the Sanskrit Āryaprajñāpāramitānāmāṣṭaśatakaṃ and the Tibetan Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa'i mtshan brgya rtsa brgyad pa. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of texts and takes the form of a devotional hymn enumerating one hundred and eight names and epithets of the Perfection of Wisdom, personified as the mother of all buddhas across past, present, and future. Opening with a verse of homage to this "Blessed Lady," the text then proceeds to enumerate her names in rapid succession, covering qualities such as omniscience, suchness, emptiness, and signlessness. As part of the Kangyur, it sits within the vast Prajñāpāramitā scriptural tradition and reflects the deeply devotional as well as philosophical dimensions of that literature.

title: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom, Vajrapāṇi, Great Vehicle Sūtra
explainer: Toh 29 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as the Noble Perfection of Wisdom, Vajrapāṇi Sūtra, in Sanskrit as the Ārya-prajñāpāramitā-vajrapāṇi-mahāyāna-sūtra, and in Tibetan as Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa lag na rdo rje theg pa chen po'i mdo. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of texts and is set at Rājagṛha, where the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi poses questions to the Buddha about how a bodhisattva should train in the Perfection of Wisdom. The Buddha's central teaching in response is that such training rests on understanding all phenomena as without arising. The text immediately follows Toh 28, the Noble Samantabhadra Great Vehicle Sūtra, and together these short sūtras form part of the broader Prajñāpāramitā section of the Kangyur.

title: The Noble Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom, the Vajra Victory Banner
explainer: Toh 30 in the Kangyur is a Mahāyāna sūtra known in English as the Noble Perfection of Wisdom, the Vajra Victory Banner, in Sanskrit as the Ārya-prajñāpāramitā-vajra-ketu-mahāyāna-sūtra, and in Tibetan as འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་རྒྱལ་མཚན. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom class of texts, a large body of Mahāyāna scriptures concerned with the nature and practice of prajñāpāramitā, the transcendent wisdom that perceives the emptiness of all phenomena. This particular sūtra takes the form of a dialogue in which the bodhisattva Vajra Victory Banner, seated among an assembled retinue at Rājagṛha, questions the Buddha about the qualities that constitute the Perfection of Wisdom. It is one of the shorter works within the Perfection of Wisdom section of the Kangyur, presenting the teaching in a concise and direct exchange between the Buddha and the inquiring bodhisattva.

The Sūtra of Maitreya
explainer: The Sūtra of Maitreya, known in Sanskrit as the Maitrīsūtra and in Tibetan as Byams pa'i mdo, is a canonical Buddhist sūtra concerning the future buddha Maitreya, the successor to the present buddha Śākyamuni. In the text, the venerable Śāriputra addresses the Blessed One at the Nyagrodha pleasure grove beside the Rohiṇī river, asking him to describe the qualities and nature of the coming buddha, and the Blessed One responds by extolling Maitreya's immeasurable merit and boundless renown. It is Toh 35 in the Kangyur, belonging to the general class of sūtra literature, and was translated into Tibetan by Zangpo at the great temple of Palthaling.

Toh 820 in the Kangyur is a short liturgical text known in Tibetan as the Auspic
explainer: Toh 820 in the Kangyur is a short liturgical text known in Tibetan as the Auspicious Verses of the Thirty-Seven Deities, belonging to the class of Yoga Tantra. The text consists of a series of benedictory verses invoking the auspiciousness of the thirty-seven deities of the maṇḍala of the Yoga Tantra, organized around the five buddha families — Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi — along with their consorts, bodhisattvas, and retinue figures including Vajrasattva. Each verse calls upon the merit and blessings of a particular deity or group of deities and dedicates that auspiciousness to all beings in the present moment. Framed as verses requested by a divine interlocutor, the text functions as a maṅgala or auspiciousness prayer and is placed within the tantra section of the Kangyur.

Praise of the Supremely Noble
explainer: Toh 1109 in the Tengyur is a devotional hymn known in Sanskrit as the Viśiṣṭastava and in Tibetan as the Khyad par du 'phags pa'i bstod pa, meaning "The Praise of the Supremely Noble." It is a work of praise poetry addressed to the Buddha, celebrating his complete freedom from faults and his possession of every virtue, while contrasting him favorably with the gods of other traditions such as Viṣṇu and Śiva, whose celebrated qualities are reframed as deficiencies in the light of Buddhist teaching. The text belongs to the stotra genre of laudatory verse, a form widely cultivated in Indian Buddhist literature, and sits within the broader class of hymns and praises found in the Tengyur.

title: A Detailed Commentary on the Hymn of Extraordinary Praise
explainer: Toh 1110 in the Tengyur is a Sanskrit and Tibetan commentary known in Sanskrit as the Viśeṣastava-nāma-ṭīkā and in Tibetan as the Khyad par du 'phags pa'i bstod pa'i rgya cher bshad pa, rendered in English as A Detailed Commentary on the Hymn of Extraordinary Praise. It is an explanatory treatise that provides a full, verse-by-verse exegesis of a hymn of praise to the Buddha composed by a brahmin named Mthobtsun Drubjé, who is said to have converted to the Buddha's teaching and expressed his devotion in poetic form. The commentary unfolds both the narrative background and the doctrinal meaning of the hymn, situating the praise within a broader religious and literary context. As a work of exegetical literature devoted to a stotra, or hymn of praise, it belongs to the class of commentarial texts preserved in the Tengyur, the canonical collection of Indian and Tibetan scholarly treatises that accompanies the Kangyur.

title: A Hymn to the Omniscient Great Lord
explainer: Toh 1111 in the Tengyur is a devotional hymn in Sanskrit known as the Sarvajñamahāśvarastotra, rendered in Tibetan as Thamché Khyenpa Wangchuk, meaning "A Hymn to the Omniscient Great Lord." It is a stotra, or praise poem, addressed to a supreme lord described in terms that blend Buddhist and Śaiva imagery — honoring a being who is a god beyond gods, the guru of gurus, the burner of the three cities, and the bearer of a skull — evoking the figure of Śiva recast within a Buddhist devotional framework. The text belongs to the broader category of hymns and praises found in the Tengyur. According to its colophon, no Indian commentary was available to the translators, and the work was completed at the monastery of glorious Sakya by the Śākya monk Kunga Gyaltsen Palzangpo.

title: Praise as Supremely Excellent Among Gods
explainer: Toh 1112 in the Tengyur is a devotional hymn known in Sanskrit as the Deva Atiśaya Stotra and in Tibetan as Lha Las Phul Du Byung Bar Bstod Pa, meaning "Praise as Supremely Excellent Among Gods." It is a stotra, or praise poem, that extols the Buddha by contrasting his qualities with those of the great Hindu deities Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva, arguing through reasoned comparison that the Buddha alone — having attained perfect peace — is truly worthy of worship. The text systematically examines the conduct, powers, and nature of these divine figures to demonstrate the Buddha's unsurpassed excellence, making it both a work of devotional literature and a form of philosophical polemic. As Toh 1112 in the Tengyur, it belongs to the collection of Indian scholarly and literary works preserved in the Tibetan Buddhist canon, falling within the category of hymns and praises composed in the classical Sanskrit stotra tradition.

title: Extensive Commentary on the Praise Surpassing the Gods
explainer: Toh 1113 in the Tengyur is an extensive Indian commentary known in Sanskrit as the Deva-atiśaya-stotra-ṭīkā and in Tibetan as the Lha las phul du byung bar bstod pa'i rgya cher 'grel pa, rendered in English as the Extensive Commentary on the Praise Surpassing the Gods. It belongs to the genre of stotra literature — works of devotional praise — and serves as a detailed exegetical commentary on a hymn celebrating the Buddha as one who surpasses even the gods, a theme developed in part through a narrative involving two brahmin brothers whose encounter with Buddhist teaching leads them to recognize the Buddha's supreme qualities. The text opens with homage to Mañjuśrī in his youthful form, a conventional dedication that situates the work within the Mahāyāna tradition. It was requested by the monk Paltsek Rakshita and definitively established in its Tibetan form, indicating it passed through the standard process of translation and editorial review that characterized the production of the Tengyur collection.
